title: Immersive Commons: Designing Ephemeral Spatial Dialogue for Co-Located Mixed Reality Environments
comment: 14 pages, 8 figures. Accepted at SIGraDi 2026, the Conference of the Iberoamerican Society of Digital Graphics
summary: Head-mounted mixed reality (MR) often prioritises individual immersion, potentially drawing attention away from others sharing the room. This paper asks how MR can support co-located spatial dialogue through embodied interaction and activity visible to non-headset observers. We introduce Immersive Commons, a design framework, and Atmos Messages, a prototype combining gesture-based, ephemeral spatial messages with voice transcription, preset text, and a public floor-plan overview. Following a Research through Design approach, fifteen participants created 236 messages across two sessions, including 48 voice-authored messages. Questionnaire responses highlighted playfulness and social awareness, while observations suggested opportunities for exchange grounded in the architectural setting. Interaction clustered near the public display, although this was also where participants put on their headsets. These findings suggest the potential of ephemeral spatial messaging to support co-located exchange, with playfulness, shared visibility, and architectural context informing the design of more social and situated MR experiences.

AI.tldr: The paper presents Immersive Commons and Atmos Messages, a mixed-reality interaction framework and prototype designed to support social, co-located communication through ephemeral spatial messages, voice transcription, preset text, and shared public visualization. A Research through Design study with 15 participants produced 236 messages and indicated that playfulness, shared visibility, and architectural context can make MR experiences more socially aware and situated.
AI.motivation: Head-mounted mixed reality can isolate users from other people in the same physical space by prioritizing individual immersion. The paper investigates how MR can instead support co-located spatial dialogue and make users’ activities legible to people without headsets.
AI.method: The authors used a Research through Design approach to develop Immersive Commons, a design framework, and Atmos Messages, a prototype enabling gesture-based ephemeral spatial messages, voice transcription, preset text, and a public floor-plan overview. Fifteen participants created 236 messages over two sessions, including 48 voice-authored messages. Questionnaires and behavioral observations were used to assess playfulness, social awareness, and interaction patterns.
AI.result: Participants generally viewed the system as playful and socially aware. Observations showed potential for communication grounded in the surrounding architecture. Interaction concentrated near the public display, though this location also served as the headset-wearing area, making the causal interpretation ambiguous.
AI.conclusion: Ephemeral spatial messaging may help transform MR from an individually immersive medium into a more social and situated experience. Effective designs should emphasize playfulness, shared visibility with non-headset observers, and meaningful integration with architectural context, while accounting for activity-location confounds in future evaluations.

title: Beyond the 1D Reality-Virtuality Continuum: A 2D Framework for Seven Extended Reality Paradigms
comment: Accepted for IndiaHCI 2026 Conference in the Student Research Consortium held at Indian Institute of Technology - Hyderabad, India; 7 pages, 4 figures
summary: The Reality-Virtuality (RV) continuum helps in describing the relationship between physical and computer-generated environments. However, the increasing number of Extended Reality (XR) paradigms introduces new technologies. Their characteristics cannot be completely represented by a single real-virtual dimension. It can be noted that XR systems not only vary in their proportion of real and virtual content but also adds, suppresses, or transforms information available to the user. This work proposes a framework for characterizing seven XR realities, namely Virtual Reality (VR), Augmented Reality (AR), Mixed Reality (MR), Augmented Virtuality (AV), Phenomenal Reality (PR), Annexing Reality (AnR), and Diminished Reality (DR). It uses a two-dimensional extension of the conventional 1D RV continuum. The first dimension helps in identification of the position of an XR technology between real and virtual environments. The second dimension captures information addition and subtraction. The proposed approach gives a qualitative basis for comparing existing and emerging XR paradigms within a unified XR framework.

AI.tldr: The paper extends the traditional one-dimensional Reality–Virtuality continuum into a two-dimensional framework to classify seven XR realities according to both their real–virtual composition and their modification of available information.
AI.motivation: The conventional Reality–Virtuality continuum primarily describes how much of an experience is real versus computer-generated. As XR technologies increasingly add, remove, or transform user-accessible information, this single dimension is insufficient to represent their distinctions. A unified framework is therefore needed to compare established and emerging XR paradigms.
AI.method: The authors propose a qualitative two-dimensional XR framework. One dimension locates a system between real and virtual environments, while the second represents information modification, including the addition and subtraction of information. Using this framework, they characterize seven realities: Virtual Reality, Augmented Reality, Mixed Reality, Augmented Virtuality, Phenomenal Reality, Annexing Reality, and Diminished Reality.
AI.result: The framework provides a unified qualitative basis for distinguishing and comparing the seven XR realities. It captures differences that cannot be represented solely by the proportion of real and virtual content, particularly whether information is added, suppressed, or transformed.
AI.conclusion: A two-dimensional extension of the Reality–Virtuality continuum offers a broader and more expressive model for organizing XR paradigms. The proposed framework supports systematic comparison of existing and future XR technologies, although the abstract reports a conceptual framework rather than empirical validation.

title: Translating Poetic Emotion into Dynamic Mathematical Visuals: A Strange Attractor-Based Approach
comment: 6 pages, 5 figures, Going to be presented for the Student Research Consortium (SRC) at India HCI 2026 (Indian Institute of Technology, Hyderabad)
summary: Poetry conveys emotional experiences through language. This project investigates how poetic emotional experiences can be represented through dynamic mathematical visualisations while further developing a pipeline for this purpose. By leveraging a pretrained RoBERTa-based emotion classifier, the system analyses the fine-grained emotional states within a poem. These detected emotions are then mapped onto the parameters of strange attractors, complex structures from dynamical systems theory, to generate abstract, deterministic, and dynamic imagery. This work situates itself at the intersection of poetry, psychology, and mathematics, aiming to extend the poetic experience beyond language into the sensory domain

AI.tldr: The paper presents a pipeline that transforms fine-grained emotional states detected in poetry into dynamic visualisations using strange attractors. A pretrained RoBERTa-based emotion classifier supplies the emotional input, while dynamical-systems mathematics generates abstract, deterministic imagery intended to extend poetic experience into the sensory domain.
AI.motivation: The work is motivated by the desire to represent and experience poetic emotion beyond linguistic interpretation. It addresses the challenge of translating nuanced, time-varying emotional states in poems into visual forms, while connecting computational emotion analysis with psychology, mathematics, and artistic expression.
AI.method: The system processes a poem with a pretrained RoBERTa-based emotion classifier to identify fine-grained emotional states. These emotion outputs are mapped to parameters of strange attractors—complex structures from dynamical systems theory—which produce abstract, deterministic, and dynamic visual imagery. The project also develops an end-to-end pipeline for performing this translation from text to visualisation.
AI.result: The abstract indicates that the project successfully establishes a conceptual and technical pipeline for converting detected poetic emotions into dynamic mathematical visualisations. It demonstrates the feasibility of using emotion classification and strange-attractor parameterisation to create evolving imagery, although it does not report quantitative evaluation, user studies, or comparative results.
AI.conclusion: The work proposes an interdisciplinary approach for extending poetry from language into sensory experience. By combining transformer-based emotion recognition with dynamical-systems visualisation, it offers a foundation for computationally mediated poetic expression, while leaving the perceptual validity and effectiveness of the generated imagery for further evaluation.

title: Externalizing Hand Grip Pressure Through Real-Time Visual Feedback
summary: Grip pressure, including contact force and its distribution across the hand, is central to skilled grasping but is not directly visible. This makes it difficult to teach, learn, and self-correct in grip-dependent motor tasks, where verbal instruction and tactile demonstration provide only partial guidance and no real-time, spatially resolved feedback tied to the learner's own grip. Using an instrumented glove, we compare pressure feedback visualizations for such guidance, evaluating how visualization type and, secondarily, sensor-region mapping shape pressure-matching performance in novices. In a study using baseball and table tennis as representative grip tasks (N=28), we find that a continuous gradient visualization produces significantly more accurate pressure matches and lower gaze entropy than a discrete bar display, despite participants perceiving the bar as more precise for pressure magnitude. Perceived precision and objective performance therefore diverged: the encoding participants judged more precise was not the one they matched more accurately with. Grip-tailored sensor-region mappings further reduced perceived temporal demand and effort, although this subjective workload advantage did not extend to objective matching accuracy. Overall, continuous pressure feedback supported more accurate grip matching and more concentrated viewing, and we present design considerations for real-time pressure feedback in motor skill guidance.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates how visual feedback designs for grip pressure affect novices’ ability to reproduce target grips. In a study of 28 participants performing baseball and table-tennis grip tasks, continuous gradient feedback yielded more accurate pressure matching and lower gaze entropy than discrete bar feedback, even though participants believed the bars conveyed pressure magnitude more precisely. Grip-specific sensor-region mappings lowered perceived effort and temporal demand but did not improve objective matching accuracy.
AI.motivation: Grip pressure and its spatial distribution are important for skilled grasping but are normally invisible to learners. Existing verbal and tactile instruction does not provide real-time, spatially resolved feedback linked to the learner’s own grip, limiting learning and self-correction in grip-dependent motor tasks. The study therefore addresses how pressure feedback should be visualized and mapped to support effective motor guidance.
AI.method: The researchers used an instrumented glove to capture grip pressure and compared two visualizations: a continuous gradient display and a discrete bar display. Twenty-eight novices performed representative baseball and table-tennis grip-matching tasks. The study examined visualization type as the primary factor and sensor-region mapping as a secondary factor. Outcomes included objective pressure-matching accuracy, gaze entropy, perceived precision, temporal demand, and effort.
AI.result: Continuous gradient feedback produced significantly more accurate pressure matches and lower gaze entropy than the discrete bar display, indicating better performance and more concentrated visual attention. Participants nevertheless perceived the bar display as more precise for judging pressure magnitude, revealing a mismatch between subjective judgments and objective performance. Grip-tailored sensor-region mappings reduced perceived temporal demand and effort, but did not improve objective matching accuracy.
AI.conclusion: For real-time grip-pressure guidance, continuous gradient visualizations appear more effective than discrete bars for accurate matching and focused viewing, despite lower perceived precision. Feedback should therefore be evaluated using behavioral performance rather than subjective preference alone. Grip-specific mappings may improve perceived usability and workload, but their objective benefits require further investigation.

title: Science-Fiction Transformation as a Design Lens for Visualization Transformation
summary: Science fiction often features characters or objects that undergo radical changes in form while still being recognizable as the same entity. For example, a vehicle might unfold into a robot, or one body might flow or shape-shift into another. We use such transformations as a reflective lens to study similar shape-shifting in visualization, where one visual representation transforms into a completely different one. For example, a node-link diagram might transform into a parallel coordinates plot as a user's task changes from understanding relationships to identifying correlations. Based on four instances of science-fiction transformation, our paper highlights two key questions: First, why is a transformation into a target form needed, or what is the purpose? Second, what remains recognizable across the transformation from source to target, or what is the correspondence? Through four hypothetical transitions between visual representations of a multifaceted dataset, we demonstrate that purpose is also essential to visualization transformations. Furthermore, we show that the question of correspondence results in different levels of complexity in terms of designing and understanding transitions. Depending on whether correspondence is 1:1, 1:N, or N:1, visualization transformations may be direct and easy to understand, or they may require more elaborate transition constructs, implying increased cognitive effort for interpretation. Particularly, cases of 1:N and N:1 correspondence pose challenges for designing visualization transformations.

AI.tldr: The paper uses science-fiction shape-shifting as a conceptual lens for studying visualization transformations. It argues that effective transformations depend on two design questions: the purpose of changing representation and the correspondence preserved between source and target. One-to-one mappings are relatively simple, whereas one-to-many and many-to-one mappings require more complex transition designs and impose greater cognitive demands.
AI.motivation: Visualization systems often need to change representations as users’ analytical tasks change, but the principles for designing and understanding such transformations are not fully articulated. The paper is motivated by the need to clarify why a visualization should transform into a particular target form and what information or identity should remain recognizable during the transition.
AI.method: The authors draw on four examples of science-fiction transformations as a reflective analogy. They then examine four hypothetical transitions between visual representations of a multifaceted dataset, analyzing each transition in terms of its purpose and its source-to-target correspondence. The correspondence types considered are 1:1, 1:N, and N:1.
AI.result: The analysis shows that transformation purpose is fundamental, not merely the visual mechanics of changing form. It also finds that correspondence determines transition complexity: 1:1 mappings can support direct, comprehensible transformations, while 1:N and N:1 mappings require more elaborate transition constructs and create greater cognitive effort. These latter cases are especially challenging for visualization design.
AI.conclusion: Visualization transformations should be designed around both the analytical purpose of the target representation and the correspondence maintained across the transition. The paper provides a conceptual framework for reasoning about transition difficulty and highlights 1:N and N:1 mappings as important areas for further design research.

title: Peers4U: Designing Learner-Centered Virtual Peers for Children's Multimodal Mathematics Learning
summary: In early mathematics, children learn abstract concepts through concrete representations, such as manipulating objects, drawing, and speaking. Learning with peers can enrich this process by exposing children to diverse strategies and enabling them to exchange ideas through interaction. We realized this potential with virtual peers in Peers4U, a multimodal learning system to enhance children's mathematical conceptual understanding. Virtual peers driven by LLMs are personalized to the learner's cognitive level and assigned multimodal solutions with inspectable processes. During learning, peers engage in mixed-initiative interactions by responding, initiating topics, and advancing discussions along a pedagogical progression. A user study with 22 children and two experts showed our learner-centered topic orchestration significantly outperformed a persona-centered baseline, and children spontaneously authored new artifacts to demonstrate inspired ideas or share their own strategies, producing significantly more solutions when grouped with more Leading Peers. We contribute design insights for multimodal, learner-centered virtual peer systems.

AI.tldr: Peers4U is a multimodal learning system that uses personalized LLM-driven virtual peers to support children's mathematical conceptual learning through mixed-initiative interaction. A study with 22 children and two experts found that learner-centered topic orchestration outperformed a persona-centered baseline, and that groups with more Leading Peers generated more solutions.
AI.motivation: Young children often learn abstract mathematics more effectively when concepts are grounded in concrete, multimodal representations. Peer interaction can further support learning by exposing children to alternative strategies and enabling collaborative idea exchange, but coordinating productive peer discussion is challenging. The paper addresses this challenge through personalized virtual peers that can interact, demonstrate inspectable reasoning processes, and support learner-centered mathematical exploration.
AI.method: The authors developed Peers4U, a multimodal learning system featuring LLM-driven virtual peers personalized to each learner's cognitive level. Peers were assigned multimodal solutions with inspectable processes and participated in mixed-initiative dialogue: they could respond to children, initiate topics, and advance discussions according to a pedagogical progression. The system was evaluated in a user study involving 22 children and two experts. A learner-centered topic-orchestration strategy was compared with a persona-centered baseline, and the effect of grouping learners with different numbers of Leading Peers was examined.
AI.result: Learner-centered topic orchestration significantly outperformed the persona-centered baseline. Children also spontaneously created new artifacts to express inspired ideas or share personal strategies. Groups containing more Leading Peers produced significantly more solutions.
AI.conclusion: Personalized virtual peers can facilitate children's mathematical conceptual understanding by combining multimodal representations, inspectable solution processes, and adaptive mixed-initiative interaction. The findings suggest that orchestration should prioritize learners' evolving ideas rather than relying mainly on fixed peer personas, and that peer-role composition can influence creative solution generation. The work contributes design insights for multimodal, learner-centered virtual peer systems.

title: An Interactive Mobile Augmented Reality System for Efficient Virtual Model-to-Patient Registration in Thoracic Surgery
summary: Video-Assisted Thoracoscopic Surgery (VATS) is a minimally invasive procedure, where precise surgical port placement is vital, yet it relies heavily on surgeon experience and mental mapping of pre-operative imaging in the operating room. To address this challenge, we present an accessible, interactive mobile augmented reality (AR) framework, HILMARTS, to enable accurate and efficient pre-operative virtual model-to-patient registration for AR-guided surgical navigation. Our system runs on a commercially available LiDAR-equipped iPad and supports a user-in-the-loop workflow through a two-stage coarse-to-fine registration process. First, the user performs a manual alignment using the AR view on the iPad. This initial maneuver is then refined through automatic point-cloud registration leveraging the LiDAR sensor. We further introduce a novel occupancy-grid-based Surface Coverage Score to provide real-time, actionable feedback to the operator on the geometric completeness of LiDAR data capture for reliable point-cloud-based alignment. In a phantom study with 16 participants, the system achieved a 3.31+/-1.26mm registration accuracy in ~4 min with a mean System Usability Scale (SUS) of 84.1. These findings highlight the system's accuracy, efficiency, robustness, and potential clinical usability, and could support its applicability to other AR-based surgical navigation tasks.

AI.tldr: HILMARTS is a mobile LiDAR-based augmented-reality framework for accurate, user-guided registration of preoperative virtual models to patients during VATS planning. It combines manual AR alignment with automatic point-cloud refinement and provides real-time feedback on scan completeness. In a 16-participant phantom study, it achieved 3.31 ± 1.26 mm accuracy in approximately 4 minutes and a mean SUS of 84.1, indicating promising usability and clinical potential.
AI.motivation: Precise surgical port placement in VATS is important but is often dependent on surgeon experience and mental transformation of preoperative imaging into the operating-room context. The paper addresses the need for an accessible, efficient, and reliable registration method that can support AR-guided surgical navigation without requiring specialized equipment or fully automated workflows.
AI.method: The authors develop HILMARTS for a commercially available LiDAR-equipped iPad. The workflow uses two-stage coarse-to-fine registration: (1) the operator manually aligns a virtual model with the patient using the iPad's AR view, and (2) LiDAR-derived point clouds are automatically registered to refine the alignment. An occupancy-grid-based Surface Coverage Score supplies real-time feedback about whether the captured LiDAR geometry is sufficiently complete for reliable registration. The system is evaluated in a phantom study with 16 participants using registration accuracy, completion time, and the System Usability Scale.
AI.result: The system achieved a registration accuracy of 3.31 ± 1.26 mm in approximately 4 minutes. It obtained a mean SUS score of 84.1, suggesting strong perceived usability. The results support the claimed accuracy, efficiency, robustness, and practicality of the user-in-the-loop workflow, although the evidence is limited to a phantom evaluation.
AI.conclusion: HILMARTS demonstrates that a consumer-grade LiDAR-equipped tablet can support accurate and usable preoperative model-to-patient registration for AR-assisted VATS navigation. Its coarse-to-fine workflow and coverage feedback may improve reliability and reduce dependence on manual judgment. Further validation in anatomical models, clinical environments, and larger participant cohorts is needed before clinical adoption.

title: Understanding Human-Robot Collaboration through Joint Action
summary: Human-robot collaboration requires partners to coordinate interdependent contributions toward a shared goal. Joint Action theory provides concepts for understanding this coordination, but how these concepts are instantiated and combined across empirical research remains fragmented. We conducted a systematic review following PRISMA 2020, identifying 83 empirical papers published between 2021 and 2026. Through theory-driven framework analysis, we organized the literature into nine constructs across three capacities: Representation, Prediction, and Integration. We analyze how these constructs are distributed and co-occur across studies, revealing where empirical evidence concentrates and where it is absent. By mapping empirical HRC research onto a unified Joint Action framework, this review offers a coherent overview of HRC studies, identifies gaps in current evidence, and provides guidelines for future research.

AI.tldr: A systematic review maps 83 empirical human–robot collaboration studies (2021–2026) onto nine Joint Action constructs grouped into Representation, Prediction, and Integration, revealing uneven evidence and research gaps.
AI.motivation: The literature applies Joint Action theory to human–robot collaboration in fragmented and inconsistent ways. The review aims to clarify how core theoretical concepts are operationalized and combined across empirical studies, while identifying underrepresented areas that limit a unified understanding of coordination.
AI.method: The authors conducted a PRISMA 2020-compliant systematic review of 83 empirical papers published from 2021 to 2026. They used theory-driven framework analysis to classify findings according to nine constructs organized under three capacities: Representation, Prediction, and Integration. They also examined construct distributions and co-occurrence patterns across studies.
AI.result: The review produces a unified mapping of empirical HRC research to the Joint Action framework. It shows that evidence is concentrated in some constructs and combinations, whereas other constructs and cross-capacity relationships receive limited attention. The abstract does not specify the exact dominant or neglected constructs, effect sizes, or quantitative distribution of studies.
AI.conclusion: Joint Action theory provides a useful integrative framework for HRC, but its empirical application remains uneven. The review identifies theoretical and evidential gaps and offers directions for designing more comprehensive future studies of human–robot coordination.

title: Comparing Temporal Deep Learning Architectures for Discrete Cross-User Myoelectric Control
summary: The recognition of dynamic gestures via discrete myoelectric control is becoming an attractive input modality for event-based human-machine interaction. While recent work suggests that discrete cross-user models are possible (i.e., no calibration data is required from the end user), few have evaluated techniques to optimize these systems and their generalizability to new randomly prompted data simulating real-world discrete control is relatively unknown. Using the 612-user EMG-EPN dataset, this work benchmarks five temporal deep-learning approaches, evaluates the tradeoff between performance and model complexity, and compares hand-crafted and machine-learned feature extraction techniques. The CNN-GRU achieved the best accuracy of 93% when tested on 184 previously unseen users. These models were then evaluated on a different, more realistic, unsegmented dataset, wherein users were randomly prompted to elicit discrete gestures during a continuous data collection. This dataset was recorded five years apart and in a separate country from the data used to train the original model. Results show that the cross-user results scale to this new dataset (accuracies of 96%) even though no feedback was given to users during the elicitation of gestures. These findings highlight the exciting potential of discrete zero-shot cross-user myoelectric control and offer valuable insights for the continued advancement of this promising technology.

AI.tldr: The paper benchmarks temporal deep-learning methods for zero-shot cross-user recognition of discrete EMG gestures and shows that a CNN-GRU can generalize well to unseen users and a separate, realistic unsegmented dataset.
AI.motivation: The study addresses the limited understanding of how to optimize discrete myoelectric control systems and whether models trained without user-specific calibration can generalize to randomly prompted, real-world-like gesture data collected under substantially different conditions.
AI.method: Using the 612-user EMG-EPN dataset, the authors benchmark five temporal deep-learning architectures, compare predictive performance with model complexity, and evaluate hand-crafted versus learned feature extraction. The strongest models are then tested on a separate unsegmented dataset collected five years later and in another country, with users randomly prompted to perform discrete gestures during continuous recording.
AI.result: The CNN-GRU achieved 93% accuracy on 184 previously unseen users. On the separate and more realistic dataset, performance reached 96%, despite differences in collection time and location and the absence of user feedback during gesture elicitation.
AI.conclusion: The results support the feasibility of zero-shot cross-user myoelectric control and indicate that temporal deep-learning models, particularly CNN-GRU architectures, can generalize beyond the original dataset to realistic continuous-control conditions.

title: Time-Dynamic Semantic-Activity Entanglement: Quantifying Communication-Based Synchrony in Collaborative VR
comment: 6 pages, 3 figures. This work has been accepted as an extended abstract in the "Poster" track for publication in the Companion Proceedings of ACM ISS 2026
summary: Collaborative virtual reality (VR) produces rich multimodal traces of team behavior, yet practical methods for characterizing time-varying team communication remain limited. We present time-dynamic semantic-activity entanglement (TSAE), inspired by the entanglement concept introduced by Gloor et al. (2022), to describe communication-based team synchronization within discrete time windows. TSAE is modeled by combining relative speaking activity with contextual semantic alignment for participant pairs, which is aggregated into participant-level trajectories and summarized through the Gini coefficient to understand the distribution of team-level communication synchrony. This approach is employed with German-language transcripts from fifteen collaborative VR gameplay sessions. Transcript utterances are represented using a long-context embedding model with a late-chunking strategy and analyzed within fixed game-time windows. A representative session illustrates shifting dyadic alignment and low-to-moderate participant contributions, with sporadic periods of high entanglement. Across fifteen game sessions, the metrics indicate complementary insights, offering a qualitative contrast to the core-periphery pattern reported in the foundational work. Hence, these descriptive findings support the study of communication as a dynamic process and provide a mathematically grounded approach to analyze its evolving distribution in shared interactive VR spaces.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces time-dynamic semantic-activity entanglement (TSAE), a windowed metric for quantifying how synchronized team communication is in collaborative VR. It combines pairwise speaking-activity similarity with semantic alignment, aggregates the measures to participants, and uses the Gini coefficient to characterize how communication synchrony is distributed across a team. Applied to German transcripts from 15 VR gameplay sessions, TSAE reveals changing dyadic relationships, generally low-to-moderate contributions, and occasional high-synchrony periods, providing a dynamic complement to prior core-periphery findings.
AI.motivation: Collaborative VR generates multimodal behavioral data, but existing approaches offer limited ways to describe how team communication synchrony changes over time and how it is distributed among participants. The paper addresses this gap by developing a mathematically grounded, interpretable measure that captures both who speaks when and how semantically aligned their contributions are.
AI.method: The study defines TSAE within discrete game-time windows. For participant pairs, it combines relative speaking activity with contextual semantic alignment. Transcript utterances from 15 German-language collaborative VR gameplay sessions are encoded with a long-context embedding model using late chunking. Pairwise measures are aggregated into participant-level trajectories, and the Gini coefficient summarizes inequality in team-level communication synchrony. A representative session is examined qualitatively, while results across all sessions are compared with the core-periphery pattern reported in prior work.
AI.result: The representative session shows time-varying dyadic semantic-activity alignment, low-to-moderate participant contributions, and intermittent periods of high entanglement. Across the 15 sessions, the metrics provide complementary descriptive information and qualitatively contrast with the previously reported core-periphery structure. The findings suggest that communication synchrony is uneven and dynamically reorganized rather than static.
AI.conclusion: TSAE offers a practical framework for studying evolving communication synchrony in shared VR environments. By jointly modeling speaking activity and semantic alignment and summarizing their distribution, it supports dynamic team-communication analysis, although the reported evidence is primarily descriptive and based on a limited set of gameplay sessions.

title: PolyGandr: Steering Generative Models via Spatial Navigation through Latent Space
summary: Generative models support content creation across text, images, videos, and design disciplines, yet their interfaces rely primarily on natural language. While effective for specifying high-level intent, language can be inefficient and imprecise for fine-grained control, iterative refinement, and open-ended exploration. We present PolyGandr, a visual interface for exploring relationships between latent representations and generated outputs, complementing natural-language model steering. PolyGandr formulates generative control as high-dimensional navigation, enabling users to define starting points, steering directions, and step sizes through a unified map-and-mixing-palette interface. Combining global exploration with local refinement supports both broad design-space navigation and fine-grained output manipulation without repeatedly translating visual intent into prompts. We evaluate PolyGandr across three use cases: StyleGAN2 face generation, Stable Diffusion chair design, and rotational kirigami engineering. A formative study indicates that PolyGandr complements existing workflows by supporting real-time editing while simultaneously providing an overview and means to explore the broader design space.

AI.tldr: PolyGandr is a visual interface for navigating generative-model latent spaces, complementing prompt-based control with global exploration and local, fine-grained refinement. A formative evaluation across faces, chair designs, and rotational kirigami suggests that it supports real-time editing while preserving an overview of the broader design space.
AI.motivation: Natural-language prompts are useful for expressing high-level intent but are inefficient and imprecise for fine-grained control, iterative refinement, and open-ended exploration. The paper addresses the need for a more direct visual method for steering generative outputs and understanding relationships between latent representations and results.
AI.method: The authors formulate generative control as high-dimensional navigation. PolyGandr provides a unified map-and-mixing-palette interface through which users specify starting points, steering directions, and step sizes. It combines global exploration of the design space with local refinement and is demonstrated with StyleGAN2 face generation, Stable Diffusion chair design, and rotational kirigami engineering.
AI.result: A formative study reports that PolyGandr complements existing workflows by enabling real-time visual editing, giving users an overview of the design space, and supporting exploration of alternative outputs without repeatedly converting visual intentions into prompts.
AI.conclusion: Visual latent-space navigation can complement natural-language steering by improving fine-grained control, iterative editing, and design-space exploration. PolyGandr demonstrates a unified interaction approach applicable across different generative models and design domains, although the abstract reports formative rather than definitive comparative evidence.

title: Who Shaped What? Untangling Human and AI Creative Contributions Through Spatial Provenance in Image Editing
summary: Images co-edited with AI are often labeled to disclose AI use. However, creators feel these labels do not sufficiently describe their contributions to the editing process. Editing histories preserve requests, suggestions, and revisions, but how do creators use these logs to judge contribution? We investigated this with Roop, a mixed-initiative design probe that links image regions to editing histories (spatial provenance) and summarizes interactions in a heat map. Twenty participants edited images, annotated human and AI contributions, then reviewed the spatial provenance heat map. Participants credited themselves for directing changes while crediting AI for determining visual details. They judged contribution partly by whether their interactions achieved their intentions. Reviewing provenance helped participants remember interactions without always changing whom they credited. These findings motivate provenance systems that preserve enough context for creators to explain how interactions shaped their work, alongside the record of what happened.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how creators assign human versus AI credit in AI-assisted image editing and how spatially linked editing histories affect those judgments. Using the Roop design probe with 20 participants, it finds that creators claim credit for directing edits, credit AI for visual detail generation, and use intention fulfillment as a key criterion. Provenance helps recall interactions but does not necessarily alter attribution, suggesting that provenance tools should explain contribution context rather than merely log actions.
AI.motivation: Existing AI-use labels disclose that AI was involved but do not adequately communicate the creator’s specific contribution. Editing logs contain richer evidence—requests, AI suggestions, and revisions—but it is unclear how creators interpret these records when deciding who contributed to the final image. The study addresses this gap by examining contribution attribution and the role of spatial provenance.
AI.method: The researchers developed Roop, a mixed-initiative design probe that connects image regions to their associated editing histories and represents interaction patterns through a heat map. Twenty participants edited images, annotated the relative contributions of themselves and the AI, and then reviewed the spatial provenance visualization. Their attribution judgments and reflections were analyzed.
AI.result: Participants generally credited themselves for setting goals and directing the editing process, while crediting the AI for determining specific visual details. They also judged contribution according to whether an interaction successfully achieved their intended outcome. Reviewing the provenance visualization improved memory of prior interactions, but it did not consistently change participants’ attribution judgments.
AI.conclusion: AI contribution disclosures should go beyond a simple indication that AI was used. Provenance systems should preserve and present enough contextual information to explain how human intentions, AI actions, and revisions jointly shaped the result. The paper emphasizes explanatory provenance—capturing the meaning and influence of interactions—not only an action history.
